reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is an instructional coding tutorial demonstrating how to create an ERC-20 token, deploy it on a test network, and add liquidity on Uniswap. It promotes an optional blockchain-development bootcamp, but does not solicit viewers to send money, buy a purported investment, or provide private data in exchange for guaranteed returns. The discussion of trading and token creation is presented as technical education and demonstration rather than deceptive financial solicitation.

opening.argument: The video links a potentially valuable outcome directly to creating and distributing a new token. It says blockchain work is “potentially worth a lot of money,” then teaches viewers to launch their own cryptocurrency, place it in a wallet, list it on an exchange, and get others trading it. That is more than neutral coding theory: it presents token creation and market participation as a rapid path toward a potentially valuable asset. The description then supplies a bootcamp URL and a GitHub code link, giving viewers concrete routes to continue. The combination of a money-related promise, a token-launch workflow, and an external conversion path supports treating the promotion as an inducement to participate in a token ecosystem.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material a tutorial does not remove the commercial and financial thrust. The video does not merely explain existing tokens; it demonstrates how to create one, list it, and enable trading. Saying that viewers may need more ETH does not negate the participation pathway. The central promise remains that a viewer can rapidly put a cryptocurrency into live circulation, while the description directs viewers to a paid-looking bootcamp destination.

citations.quote: now anybody can buy your token

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted money language does not promise that viewers will earn money by buying or holding a token. The actual demonstration is programming instruction: it creates a contract, assigns balances, and uses a test network. The video explicitly limits the demonstration’s trading capacity, saying viewers “won't be able to buy many tokens.” Listing a self-created test token is not evidence of an appreciation claim or a solicitation to purchase it.

citations.quote: for this demo purposes, you won't be able to buy many tokens
Today, I've got a brand new coding tutorial video for you. I'm going to give you an introduction to blockchain development with Ethereum. And the Solidity programming language.

opening.argument: Several unusually strong risk signals appear together. The video says even someone with “zero coding experience” can follow along, describes launching a cryptocurrency and getting people trading “really fast,” and says the activity may be worth a lot of money. It also uses crypto wallets, an exchange, liquidity, and external links. Those elements lower the apparent barrier while emphasizing speed and possible value, creating a persuasive impression that viewers can quickly create and promote a tradable asset. The technical framing can make the proposition look credible without establishing that the resulting token has legitimate value, demand, or protection for participants.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The disclaimer that the example has limited liquidity is itself evidence that the video is discussing an actual trading setup, not merely abstract code. The presenter still walks viewers through funding a liquidity pool and swapping ETH for the token. Technical screens and test-network references may show procedure, but they do not answer the concern that the presentation pairs low barriers, speed, possible wealth, and crypto participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are not claims of guaranteed returns or evidence that viewers are asked to buy an investment. “Zero coding experience” describes accessibility of the lesson, while “potentially worth a lot of money” is expressly qualified. The walkthrough uses a test network and even says the demonstration cannot support many purchases. Crypto terminology and external educational links are not, by themselves, proof of deceptive financial solicitation.

opening.argument: The educational label masks a promotional funnel. The speaker repeatedly presents blockchain mastery, rapid deployment, live trading, and potentially substantial value, then directs viewers to a bootcamp. The lesson is therefore not only explaining how smart contracts work; it is showcasing a simple route from beginner status to launching a tradable cryptocurrency and encouraging further participation through the linked program. The invitation is especially promotional because the video says it is for everybody, including people with no coding experience, while presenting token creation and exchange listing as achievable quickly. That framing steers inexperienced viewers toward an asset-creation and trading ecosystem under the authority of an instructional demonstration.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The presence of code does not settle the role of the whole video. The presenter concludes by promoting further courses and a path to becoming a blockchain developer, after demonstrating a token that can be traded. That progression turns the tutorial into a recruitment and participation vehicle: beginners are shown a fast, valuable-looking result and then directed onward. The instructional format can increase persuasion rather than neutralize it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The closing promotion is for blockchain-development education, not for purchasing the demonstrated token or sending funds to the presenter. The lesson teaches Solidity, contract deployment, balances, and liquidity mechanics, and the exchange activity occurs on a test network. The fact that an instructional creator advertises additional courses does not transform technical education into a claim that viewers will profit from holding an asset.
